title: Organic Chemistry II
source_note: Standard NUC-aligned Nigerian university 200L organic chemistry curriculum, second semester, continuing directly from CHM205: carbonyl compounds (aldehydes and ketones), carboxylic acids and their derivatives (acyl chlorides, anhydrides, esters, amides), aromatic chemistry (benzene, aromaticity, electrophilic aromatic substitution and directing effects), amines, and key named reactions (Grignard, aldol, Cannizzaro, Friedel-Crafts, diazotization). Hydrocarbons, alcohols, haloalkanes, isomerism, and basic SN1/SN2/addition mechanisms are covered in CHM205 and not repeated here.

questions.question: What is the characteristic functional group common to both aldehydes and ketones?
questions.correct_answer: The carbonyl group, C=O
questions.explanation: Both aldehydes and ketones contain the carbonyl functional group (C=O); they differ in that an aldehyde has at least one hydrogen attached to the carbonyl carbon while a ketone has two carbon substituents.

questions.question: What is the IUPAC name of CH3CH2CHO?
questions.correct_answer: Propanal
questions.explanation: CH3CH2CHO is a three-carbon chain with a terminal -CHO group, named propanal according to IUPAC rules for aldehydes (suffix -al).

questions.question: Why is the carbonyl carbon of an aldehyde or ketone particularly susceptible to attack by nucleophiles?
options: Oxygen's higher electronegativity polarizes the C=O bond, leaving the carbon with a partial positive charge
The carbonyl carbon carries a full negative charge
Carbonyl compounds have no polarity at all
The oxygen atom is electron-poor relative to carbon
questions.correct_answer: Oxygen's higher electronegativity polarizes the C=O bond, leaving the carbon with a partial positive charge
questions.explanation: Oxygen is more electronegative than carbon, so the C=O bond is polarized with a partial positive charge on carbon, making it electrophilic and open to attack by nucleophiles in addition reactions.

questions.question: Tollens' test is used to distinguish an aldehyde from a ketone. What is the positive result of this test?
options: Formation of a silver mirror on the inside of the test tube
The solution turns from orange to colourless
A yellow precipitate of triiodomethane forms
questions.correct_answer: Formation of a silver mirror on the inside of the test tube
questions.explanation: Tollens' reagent (ammoniacal silver nitrate) oxidizes aldehydes to carboxylic acids while the Ag+ ions are reduced to metallic silver, depositing a characteristic silver mirror; ketones do not react.

questions.question: Fehling's solution gives a brick-red precipitate with aliphatic aldehydes but not with aromatic aldehydes such as benzaldehyde. What is the brick-red precipitate?
questions.correct_answer: Copper(I) oxide, Cu2O
questions.explanation: Fehling's solution contains Cu2+ complexed with tartrate; aliphatic aldehydes reduce Cu2+ to Cu+, precipitating as brick-red copper(I) oxide, while aromatic aldehydes lack the reactivity to give a positive result.

questions.question: The iodoform test gives a yellow precipitate with methyl ketones (compounds containing the CH3-CO- group). What is the yellow precipitate formed?
questions.correct_answer: Triiodomethane (iodoform), CHI3
questions.explanation: Iodine and sodium hydroxide react with compounds containing a methyl ketone (or a secondary alcohol/ethanal that can be oxidized to one) to give a distinctive yellow precipitate of triiodomethane (iodoform).

questions.question: What product is formed when an aldehyde is reduced with a reducing agent such as sodium borohydride (NaBH4)?
questions.correct_answer: A primary alcohol
questions.explanation: Reduction of an aldehyde adds hydrogen across the C=O bond, converting the carbonyl into a -CH2OH group, giving a primary alcohol.

questions.question: What product is formed when a ketone is reduced with a reducing agent such as lithium aluminium hydride (LiAlH4)?
questions.correct_answer: A secondary alcohol
questions.explanation: Reduction of a ketone converts the carbonyl carbon (bonded to two other carbons) into a carbon bearing an -OH group and two carbon substituents, giving a secondary alcohol.

questions.question: When a Grignard reagent (RMgX) reacts with formaldehyde (HCHO) followed by acidic workup, what type of alcohol is obtained?
questions.correct_answer: A primary alcohol
questions.explanation: Grignard reagents add to the carbonyl carbon of formaldehyde; since formaldehyde has two hydrogens on its carbonyl carbon, the product after aqueous acid workup is a primary alcohol with one new C-C bond.

questions.question: Reaction of a Grignard reagent with a ketone, followed by acidic workup, produces which type of alcohol?
questions.correct_answer: A tertiary alcohol
questions.explanation: Ketones already bear two carbon substituents on the carbonyl carbon; addition of the Grignard reagent's carbon nucleophile gives a third carbon substituent, so acidic workup yields a tertiary alcohol.

questions.question: What structural feature must an aldehyde or ketone possess to undergo a base-catalyzed aldol condensation?
options: At least one hydrogen atom on the carbon alpha to the carbonyl group
A minimum of two carbonyl groups in the same molecule
An aromatic ring directly attached to the carbonyl carbon
A halogen substituent on the carbonyl carbon
questions.correct_answer: At least one hydrogen atom on the carbon alpha to the carbonyl group
questions.explanation: Aldol condensation requires removal of an acidic alpha-hydrogen by base to form an enolate, which then attacks the carbonyl carbon of a second carbonyl molecule; compounds lacking alpha-hydrogens cannot form this enolate.

questions.question: Aldehydes lacking an alpha-hydrogen, such as benzaldehyde or formaldehyde, undergo the Cannizzaro reaction in concentrated base. What happens in this reaction?
options: One molecule of the aldehyde is oxidized to a carboxylate while another is reduced to an alcohol (disproportionation)
The aldehyde is simply reduced to a primary alcohol
Two aldehyde molecules combine via aldol condensation
The aldehyde is converted directly into a ketone
questions.correct_answer: One molecule of the aldehyde is oxidized to a carboxylate while another is reduced to an alcohol (disproportionation)
questions.explanation: In the Cannizzaro reaction, hydroxide attacks the carbonyl carbon and a hydride is transferred between two aldehyde molecules that lack alpha-hydrogens, simultaneously oxidizing one to a carboxylate salt and reducing the other to an alcohol.

questions.question: Why are carboxylic acids significantly more acidic than alcohols with a similar carbon skeleton?
options: The negative charge on the carboxylate ion formed after deprotonation is delocalized (resonance-stabilized) over two oxygen atoms
Carboxylic acids contain more hydrogen atoms than alcohols
Alcohols contain a carbonyl group that stabilizes their conjugate base
Carboxylic acids do not ionize in water at all
questions.correct_answer: The negative charge on the carboxylate ion formed after deprotonation is delocalized (resonance-stabilized) over two oxygen atoms
questions.explanation: Loss of a proton from a carboxylic acid gives a carboxylate ion in which the negative charge is delocalized equally over both oxygen atoms by resonance, stabilizing the conjugate base and making the acid far more acidic than an alcohol, whose alkoxide conjugate base has no such delocalization.

questions.question: Which reaction is commonly used to prepare a carboxylic acid directly from a primary alcohol?
options: Full oxidation with excess acidified potassium dichromate under reflux
questions.correct_answer: Full oxidation with excess acidified potassium dichromate under reflux
questions.explanation: Vigorous oxidation of a primary alcohol with excess acidified dichromate under reflux proceeds through the aldehyde intermediate all the way to the carboxylic acid.

questions.question: In Fischer esterification, a carboxylic acid reacts with an alcohol in the presence of an acid catalyst (such as concentrated H2SO4) to form an ester. What is the other product of this reaction?
questions.correct_answer: Water
questions.explanation: Fischer esterification is an acid-catalyzed, reversible condensation between a carboxylic acid and an alcohol, eliminating water to form the ester (RCOOR').

questions.question: What is the term for the base-catalyzed hydrolysis of an ester, which produces a carboxylate salt and an alcohol and is used industrially to make soap?
questions.correct_answer: Saponification
questions.explanation: Saponification is the alkaline hydrolysis of an ester (such as a fat or oil, a triester of glycerol), which is irreversible and yields the carboxylate salt (soap) plus the free alcohol (glycerol).

questions.question: Among carboxylic acid derivatives (acyl chlorides, anhydrides, esters, amides), which is generally the most reactive towards nucleophilic acyl substitution?
questions.correct_answer: Acyl chlorides
questions.explanation: Acyl chlorides are the most reactive carboxylic acid derivatives because chloride is an excellent leaving group and provides little resonance stabilization to the carbonyl, making the carbonyl carbon highly electrophilic; the general reactivity order is acyl chloride > anhydride > ester > amide.

questions.question: Which reagent is commonly used to convert a carboxylic acid into the corresponding acyl chloride?
questions.correct_answer: Thionyl chloride (SOCl2)
questions.explanation: Thionyl chloride (or phosphorus pentachloride, PCl5) converts the -OH of a carboxylic acid into -Cl, producing the acyl chloride along with sulfur dioxide and hydrogen chloride gas.

questions.question: What product forms when an acyl chloride reacts with excess ammonia?
questions.correct_answer: A primary amide
questions.explanation: Ammonia acts as a nucleophile, displacing chloride from the acyl chloride to form a primary amide (RCONH2), with a second equivalent of ammonia neutralizing the HCl by-product.

questions.question: According to Huckel's rule, how many delocalized pi electrons must a planar, fully conjugated cyclic system have to be considered aromatic?
options: 4n + 2, where n is a non-negative integer (e.g., 6 for benzene)
Any even number of pi electrons
4n, where n is a non-negative integer
questions.correct_answer: 4n + 2, where n is a non-negative integer (e.g., 6 for benzene)
questions.explanation: Huckel's rule states that a planar, fully conjugated monocyclic system is aromatic if it contains 4n+2 delocalized pi electrons; benzene satisfies this with n=1, giving 6 pi electrons.

questions.question: Why are all six carbon-carbon bonds in benzene of equal length, intermediate between a typical single and double bond?
options: The pi electrons are delocalized equally around the ring rather than being fixed as alternating single and double bonds
Benzene has no double bonds at all
Benzene's ring alternates rapidly between two Kekule structures at room temperature only under UV light
Each carbon atom in benzene is sp3 hybridized
questions.correct_answer: The pi electrons are delocalized equally around the ring rather than being fixed as alternating single and double bonds
questions.explanation: Benzene's true structure is a resonance hybrid in which the six pi electrons are delocalized evenly over all six carbons, giving six equivalent carbon-carbon bonds of intermediate length rather than three distinct single and three distinct double bonds.

questions.question: What is the general mechanism by which benzene reacts with electrophiles such as NO2+ or Br+?
options: Electrophilic aromatic substitution, via an arenium (Wheland) intermediate followed by loss of a proton
Electrophilic addition, saturating the ring completely
questions.correct_answer: Electrophilic aromatic substitution, via an arenium (Wheland) intermediate followed by loss of a proton
questions.explanation: Benzene's electron-rich pi system attacks an electrophile to form a resonance-stabilized, non-aromatic arenium cation intermediate, which then loses a proton to restore aromaticity, giving an overall substitution rather than addition product.

questions.question: In the nitration of benzene using concentrated nitric and sulfuric acids, which species acts as the electrophile that attacks the ring?
questions.correct_answer: The nitronium ion, NO2+
questions.explanation: Concentrated sulfuric acid protonates nitric acid and facilitates loss of water to generate the nitronium ion, NO2+, which is the actual electrophile that attacks the benzene ring in nitration.

questions.question: In Friedel-Crafts alkylation, an alkyl halide reacts with benzene in the presence of a Lewis acid catalyst such as AlCl3. What is the main limitation of this reaction with primary alkyl halides bearing beta-hydrogens?
options: Carbocation rearrangement can occur, giving a mixture of alkylated products
The reaction produces only aromatic aldehydes
Benzene cannot react with any alkyl halide under these conditions
The product is always a carboxylic acid instead of an alkylbenzene
questions.correct_answer: Carbocation rearrangement can occur, giving a mixture of alkylated products
questions.explanation: Friedel-Crafts alkylation proceeds through a carbocation intermediate generated by the Lewis acid; primary carbocations readily rearrange (via hydride or alkyl shifts) to more stable secondary or tertiary cations, often giving a mixture of rearranged alkylation products.

questions.question: Friedel-Crafts acylation (using an acyl chloride and AlCl3) is often preferred over Friedel-Crafts alkylation when a single, unrearranged product is desired. Why?
options: The acylium ion intermediate is resonance-stabilized and does not rearrange
Acylation does not require a Lewis acid catalyst
Acylation always produces an aromatic amine
The acyl chloride reacts without forming any cationic intermediate
questions.correct_answer: The acylium ion intermediate is resonance-stabilized and does not rearrange
questions.explanation: The acylium ion (RCO+) formed from the acyl chloride and AlCl3 is stabilized by resonance delocalization of the positive charge onto oxygen, so it does not undergo the rearrangements seen with simple alkyl carbocations, giving a single, predictable ketone product.

questions.question: Substituents such as -OH, -NH2, and alkyl groups already present on a benzene ring direct further electrophilic substitution mainly to which positions?
options: They have no directing effect at all
questions.correct_answer: Ortho and para positions
questions.explanation: Electron-donating groups such as -OH, -NH2, and alkyl substituents increase electron density most at the ortho and para positions (through resonance or inductive donation), directing incoming electrophiles there and generally activating the ring toward further substitution.

questions.question: Strongly electron-withdrawing substituents such as -NO2 and -COOH direct further electrophilic aromatic substitution mainly to which position, while also deactivating the ring?
questions.correct_answer: Meta position
questions.explanation: Electron-withdrawing groups destabilize the arenium intermediate most severely when the positive charge would be placed on the carbon bearing the substituent (as occurs for ortho/para attack), so meta attack is comparatively favoured, and the strong electron withdrawal also deactivates the whole ring toward electrophiles.

questions.question: Halogens (such as -Cl on chlorobenzene) are unusual substituents because they are ortho/para-directing yet deactivate the ring toward electrophilic substitution. What explains this combination?
options: The halogen withdraws electron density inductively (deactivating) but donates a lone pair by resonance into the ring at ortho/para positions (directing)
Halogens have no electronic effect on the ring at all
Halogens are purely electron-donating groups with no inductive effect
Halogens react only through free-radical mechanisms, not electrophilic substitution
questions.correct_answer: The halogen withdraws electron density inductively (deactivating) but donates a lone pair by resonance into the ring at ortho/para positions (directing)
questions.explanation: A halogen's strong electronegativity withdraws electron density inductively, deactivating the ring overall, but its lone pairs can be donated into the ring by resonance, which stabilizes the arenium intermediate more effectively for ortho/para attack than for meta attack.

questions.question: Why is aniline (a primary aromatic amine) a considerably weaker base than an aliphatic amine such as ethylamine?
options: The nitrogen lone pair in aniline is delocalized into the aromatic ring, making it less available to accept a proton
Aliphatic amines cannot act as bases at all
Aniline has a positive charge on nitrogen even before protonation
questions.correct_answer: The nitrogen lone pair in aniline is delocalized into the aromatic ring, making it less available to accept a proton
questions.explanation: In aniline, the lone pair on nitrogen is partly delocalized into the aromatic pi system by resonance, reducing its availability to bond a proton and making aniline a much weaker base than aliphatic amines, where the lone pair is fully localized on nitrogen.

questions.question: Which method is commonly used to prepare a primary aromatic amine, such as aniline, from the corresponding nitro compound?
options: Reduction of the nitro compound, e.g., with tin and concentrated hydrochloric acid
questions.correct_answer: Reduction of the nitro compound, e.g., with tin and concentrated hydrochloric acid
questions.explanation: Nitrobenzene is commonly reduced (classically using Sn/HCl or Fe/HCl, or catalytic hydrogenation) to give aniline, the corresponding primary aromatic amine.

questions.question: What is formed when a primary aromatic amine reacts with nitrous acid (generated in situ from NaNO2 and HCl) at low temperature (0-5 degC)?
questions.correct_answer: A diazonium salt
questions.explanation: Diazotization of a primary aromatic amine with cold nitrous acid produces an aryldiazonium salt (ArN2+), which is stable only at low temperature and is a key intermediate for further synthetic transformations.

questions.question: Aryldiazonium salts undergo a coupling reaction with phenols or aromatic amines to give brightly coloured compounds used as dyes. What functional group links the two aromatic rings in the product?
questions.correct_answer: An azo group, -N=N-
questions.explanation: Diazonium coupling reactions join the diazonium carbon-derived nitrogen to an electron-rich aromatic ring through an azo linkage (-N=N-), producing conjugated, highly coloured azo dyes.

questions.question: What functional group is present in a nitrile, and what is the main product of its complete acidic or basic hydrolysis?
options: The -C≡N group; hydrolysis gives a carboxylic acid (or carboxylate salt)
The -CHO group; hydrolysis gives an alcohol
The -NO2 group; hydrolysis gives an amine
The -CONH2 group; hydrolysis gives an ester
questions.correct_answer: The -C≡N group; hydrolysis gives a carboxylic acid (or carboxylate salt)
questions.explanation: Nitriles (R-C≡N) undergo hydrolysis under acidic or basic conditions, proceeding through an amide intermediate, to give a carboxylic acid (as the free acid under acidic conditions or as the carboxylate salt under basic conditions).

questions.question: What is the key difference in reactivity between an amide and an ester towards hydrolysis, and why?
options: Amides are far less readily hydrolyzed than esters because the nitrogen lone pair delocalizes more strongly into the carbonyl, reducing its electrophilicity
Amides hydrolyze more easily than esters because nitrogen is a better leaving group than an alkoxide
Both hydrolyze at identical rates under all conditions
Esters cannot be hydrolyzed under any conditions
questions.correct_answer: Amides are far less readily hydrolyzed than esters because the nitrogen lone pair delocalizes more strongly into the carbonyl, reducing its electrophilicity
questions.explanation: Nitrogen is a poorer leaving group than an alkoxide, and its lone pair donates more effectively into the carbonyl by resonance than oxygen's does in an ester, making the amide carbonyl less electrophilic and the amide bond harder to hydrolyze, requiring more forcing conditions than ester hydrolysis.

questions.question: What is formed when acetic anhydride reacts with an alcohol such as ethanol?
options: An ester (ethyl acetate) plus acetic acid
A carboxylic acid plus an alkyl halide
questions.correct_answer: An ester (ethyl acetate) plus acetic acid
questions.explanation: Anhydrides react with alcohols via nucleophilic acyl substitution, in which the alcohol's oxygen attacks the carbonyl carbon and displaces a carboxylate, giving an ester and a molecule of the corresponding carboxylic acid.

questions.question: 2,4-Dinitrophenylhydrazine (2,4-DNP, Brady's reagent) is used as a qualitative test reagent for which class of compounds?
options: Aldehydes and ketones (compounds containing a carbonyl group)
questions.correct_answer: Aldehydes and ketones (compounds containing a carbonyl group)
questions.explanation: 2,4-DNP condenses with the carbonyl group of aldehydes and ketones to form an orange or yellow crystalline hydrazone precipitate, a classic qualitative confirmatory test for the presence of a carbonyl group.

questions.question: What distinguishes an addition polymer, such as polyethylene, from a condensation polymer, such as a polyester or nylon, in terms of how monomers combine?
options: Addition polymers form by monomers joining without loss of any small molecule, while condensation polymers form with elimination of a small molecule such as water
Addition polymers always contain nitrogen atoms
Condensation polymers form only from alkenes
Addition polymers require a diacid and a diamine monomer
questions.correct_answer: Addition polymers form by monomers joining without loss of any small molecule, while condensation polymers form with elimination of a small molecule such as water
questions.explanation: Addition polymerization simply links unsaturated monomers (e.g., ethene) together with no by-product, whereas condensation polymerization joins bifunctional monomers (e.g., diacids with diols or diamines) with the repeated loss of a small molecule such as water or HCl.
